title: Galbot Robots complete 100 consecutive rallies against a tennis champion
excerpt: Galbot says its robot sustained 100 rallies against a tennis champion with no teleoperation. The claim is the company's own, and the machine is unnamed.
content_html:
Galbot says its robot completed more than 100 consecutive autonomous tennis rallies against former world number 15 Zheng Jie at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. The rally count, the autonomy claim and the robot’s identity all rest on the company’s own account.

A robot spent Saturday rallying with a former Wimbledon semi-finalist. The Beijing company Galbot says its machine sustained more than 100 consecutive exchanges against Zheng Jie at the World Humanoid Robot Games, with no teleoperation and no scripted sequence.

The described performance is not trivial. Chinese state media reported serves above 100 kilometres per hour, and said the robot fell backwards on a high looping ball and got itself upright within seconds.

Tennis is a far better test than the sprint records set at the same event. A rally demands tracking a fast object, planning a whole-body response and adapting to an opponent inside a fraction of a second, which is closer to the problem Europe’s robot makers have chosen than a straight line is.

Then there is the sourcing. The rally count, the world record framing and the no-teleoperation claim all come from Galbot’s own press release, repeated by Chinese state broadcasters, with no independent audit and no published figures on interventions or success rates.

The opponent is worth stating plainly. Zheng Jie reached a career high of world number 15 and the Wimbledon semi-finals in 2008, and she retired from professional tennis a decade ago.

The larger gap is which robot this was. No account we could find names the model, and Galbot’s commercial machine, the G1, is a wheeled dual-arm manipulator that does not have legs to fall over or stand back up on.

CGTN adds that the system was built with Tsinghua University. That is a research collaboration, which raises the possibility that the machine on court is not the machine the company sells.

What Galbot sells is unglamorous. The G1 works in warehouses, hospital pharmacies and more than 30 Chinese cities under the Galbot Store brand, on $800mn raised at a $3bn valuation, in a sector where rivals carry valuations above $2bn.

Europe is already inside that supply chain. Galbot lists Bosch among its deployment partners, alongside CATL, Toyota and Hyundai.

Bosch turns out to be on both sides of this race. The German group is also lined up to manufacture for Humanoid, the London startup that raised $152mn to build robots for factory work.

So the checkable version of this story is not on a tennis court. It is whether a wheeled robot restocks a pharmacy shelf for a year without a person fixing it, which is the thing Galbot actually sells and the thing nobody films.
